$comment: Account- and zone-level infrastructure that wrangler.jsonc cannot reach.
wrangler.jsonc already declares the compute layer (routes, crons, bindings,
DO migrations) and CI dry-runs it on every PR. This file covers the rest: the
DNS records, the resources those bindings point at, the Worker inventory, and
the release wiring. Until this existed, all of that lived in prose in
CLAUDE.md and in the Cloudflare dashboard, so a wiped record or a fat-fingered
dashboard field left no red mark anywhere in the tree.
This is a DECLARATION, not an apply path. `bun run infra:check` reads it and
diffs against reality; nothing here mutates Cloudflare. Changing a value here
does not change production, it changes what the check demands of production.
Resource IDs deliberately live in wrangler.jsonc alone. This file names what
must exist and why; the checker reads the IDs from wrangler.jsonc so the two
cannot drift into two different answers.
The Cloudflare account everything here lives in. Declared because
wrangler auto-selects an account only while the login can see exactly
one, so the whole toolchain worked for months on an accident rather than
on anything written down. On 2026-08-07 a second account showed up on
this login and every non-interactive wrangler call broke at once with
"More than one account available but unable to select one in
non-interactive mode" — deploy, deploy:version, deploy:promote,
dev:remote and routes:check:remote, none of which had changed.
Both wrangler configs pin `account_id` now and checkTree fails if they
drift from this id or from each other. The dev twin needs it for the
same reason the deploy config does: dev:remote and routes:check:remote
reach production bindings through wrangler.dev.jsonc.
The id ships SEVEN times, and checkTree reads all seven. Each of the
two site configs carries it as the deploy-time `account_id` pin and
again as the runtime
var CF_ACCOUNT_ID, which /ledger uses to query this account's own
Analytics Engine. The var predates the pin, and it is the reason there
is no ambiguity about WHICH account is right: the deployed Worker has
been reading this one's analytics all along. Wrangler has no way to
reference a value from elsewhere in its own config, so the duplication
cannot be removed — it can only be checked, which is what this block is
for. An account_id and a CF_ACCOUNT_ID that disagree would deploy to one
account and read analytics from another, with each half looking fine.
The other three are the AUXILIARY Workers, pinned 2026-08-21 after a
non-interactive deploy of lwe-ask failed on exactly the error this block
was written about. cf-garage, lwe-ask and lens-reader each deploy from
their own directory with -c wrangler.toml, so wrangler resolves the
account from THAT file and never reads wrangler.jsonc at all. Until they
were pinned the answer came from ~/.wrangler/cache/wrangler-account.json,
which only an interactive prompt writes, so whether a deploy worked
depended on machine-local cache state rather than on anything in the
repository. Measured the same day: with that cache populated cf-garage
and lwe-ask resolved fine while lens-reader still failed, which is the
shape of a guarantee nobody has.
NO ID HERE, per this file's own rule: resource ids live in wrangler.jsonc
alone and the checker reads them from there, so the two can never drift
into two different answers. wrangler.jsonc's account_id is the source of
truth and the other three copies are checked against IT, not against a
fifth copy written here. What this block declares is the invariant — all
four must agree — which is the part wrangler.jsonc cannot state about
itself.
This is the TREE tier, so it is a string comparison with no credential
and it runs on every PR. It deliberately does NOT assert that the
account exists or that a token can reach it: a token scoped to this
account cannot enumerate the others, so 'is this the right one of the
two' is not a question the API tier can answer. What the pin buys is
that the answer stops depending on how many accounts a given login
happens to see.

dnssec.why: DS is published at the registrar, so the chain of trust is out of Cloudflare's hands. If it ever stops matching, the DNS-AID SVCB answer below stops being authenticated and validating resolvers start refusing the zone outright.

$comment: The Transform Rule that pins a visitor to ONE Worker version for the
duration of a gradual deployment. Declared here for the same reason the
Workers Builds triggers are: dashboard state, load-bearing for what
reaches production, and silent when it changes.
WHAT BREAKS WITHOUT IT. Every document this site serves references
content-hashed shell assets (/a/luna.<hash8>.css, /a/nav.<hash8>.js).
build.mjs keeps exactly one hash per asset, so a version has never heard
of any other version's hashes. During a ramp each request routes
independently, /a/* is run_worker_first, and /a/ is NOT in
WORKERS_CACHEABLE_PATHS, so nothing bridges the two versions: a document
from one version asks for an asset the other version does not have and
gets serveAssetWith404Clamp's 404. At the 10% canary step that is ~90% of
the new-HTML cohort plus ~10% of the old-HTML cohort, per changed asset,
on any release that touches nav.js or luna.css. Cloudflare's own docs name
this exact case.
The 404 clamp is what keeps it from being permanent: max-age=0 means a
miss cannot pin itself at the edge under the 1-year immutable rule. That
clamp was written for /images/* (gotcha 1) and has been quietly holding
this line too.
ip.src rather than the cookie the docs prefer. A cookie needs the Worker
to mint one per visitor, which is a tracking-shaped change to a site whose
/whoareyou makes claims about what it does not collect, and a Set-Cookie on
the HTML response would take the page out of shared caches. ip.src groups
visitors behind one NAT and flips when someone changes network; neither
matters at this traffic, and both are strictly better than random.
THE EXPRESSION GUARD IS LOAD-BEARING, and it is not cosmetic. A blanket
`true` expression would overwrite a client-supplied key, and the ramp's own
split probe sends one key per request precisely so it can still observe the
split from a single IP. Clobber that and every intermediate step reads 40
of 40 on one version, which deploy-promote.mjs treats as a dead ramp. It
fails CLOSED (a false abort, never a bad release) and deploy-promote names
this rule in that error for exactly that reason.
version_affinity.why: Without version affinity a gradual deployment serves a visitor HTML from one version and content-hashed assets from another, which 404s the shell and renders an unstyled page. The check is the only thing standing between deleting this rule and finding out on the next ramp that touches nav.js.

dns.name: aadhar.sh
dns.why: The apex, proxied through Cloudflare. Public DNS shows anycast edge addresses rather than an origin, so the check asserts the shape (at least one A and one AAAA) instead of pinning IPs Cloudflare is free to rotate.

dns.name: www.aadhar.sh
dns.why: www must land on the same proxied edge as the apex.

dns.name: cal.aadhar.sh
dns.why: Backs the `cal.aadhar.sh/*` route in wrangler.jsonc. The route is declared in code but the hostname it needs is not, so without this entry the coffee module can lose its domain and every config in the repo still validates clean.

dns.name: _index._agents.aadhar.sh
dns.why: DNS-AID agent discovery (draft-mozleywilliams-dnsop-dnsaid + RFC 9460). Deliberately only _index is published, never _a2a: the site runs no Agent2Agent server, and a dangling _a2a would pass a scanner while breaking any agent that connected.
dns.gotcha: macOS ships dig 9.10.6, which does not know the SVCB mnemonic and silently degrades the query to an A lookup, reporting this record as missing when it is fine. The checker uses DoH and asks for type 64 by number.

dns.name: aadhar.sh
dns.why: The record that actually drives how a browser connects, and the DNS half of two zone toggles that have no other representation anywhere in this repo. `alpn=h3,h2` is HTTP/3 advertised in DNS (Speed > Settings > Protocol Optimization), and `ech=` is Encrypted ClientHello being on. Cloudflare generates and rotates this record; we do not author it, we assert its shape. Either toggle could be flipped in a dashboard and nothing in this tree would notice, which is the whole reason it is declared here.
dns.gotcha: Matched with `contains`, not `exact`, because Cloudflare owns the parts that move: the ech= key rotates and the ipv4/ipv6 hints change with the edge. Exact-matching would fail on every rotation; present-matching would miss the case that actually matters, which is a toggle silently dropping one parameter out of an otherwise healthy record.
dns.pairs_with: The edge tier's http3-on check. This asserts h3 is advertised in DNS; that one asserts the edge really answers with alt-svc h3. A client needs both, and either half can break alone.
dns.esni: There is deliberately no ESNI here. ESNI was the 2018 draft, it had known weaknesses, and Cloudflare removed support for it years ago. ECH is its replacement and is what `ech=` above refers to. If someone goes looking for an ESNI setting later, this is the note saying there is nothing to find.

dns.name: aadhar.sh
dns.why: Cloudflare Email Routing. coffee@aadhar.sh is the host address the booking flow sends from and the DMARC rua target, so losing MX breaks /coffee's approve/decline loop quietly.

dns.name: aadhar.sh
dns.why: SPF for the two senders that actually exist: Cloudflare Email Routing and Google. Exact-matched because this is hand-authored policy, so any change should be deliberate rather than discovered later in a spam folder.

dns.name: _dmarc.aadhar.sh
dns.why: p=reject with strict alignment on both SPF and DKIM. Strict alignment is unforgiving by design, which makes the DKIM record below load-bearing rather than optional.

dns.name: resend._domainkey.aadhar.sh
dns.why: Resend's DKIM key, which signs the /coffee confirmation and invite mail. Presence-matched, not exact: Resend owns rotation, so pinning the key would turn a routine rotation into a CI failure. Deletion still fails, which is the case that matters under adkim=s.

dns.name: default._bimi.aadhar.sh
dns.why: BIMI logo for inbox display. This record is the ONLY consumer of public/bimi.svg anywhere in the world, which is why that file reads as detritus to every reference sweep in this tree. The `consumer` field below is what closes the loop: the checker asserts the file exists, so deleting it now goes red here instead of silently breaking mail.

resources.$comment: IDs live in wrangler.jsonc. This lists what must exist in the account and why, and the checker joins the two by binding name.

kv_namespaces.title: rn-cache
kv_namespaces.why: Playlist tracks, photo manifest, artist pics, Lens screenshots, the /around crawl snapshot.

kv_namespaces.title: cal-aadhar-sh-CAL_BOOKINGS
kv_namespaces.why: Pending and confirmed coffee bookings, plus the per-slot held: keys.

r2_buckets.why: The SOOC originals, ~3GB over 158 photos. The only copy that is not on the owner's SSD.

d1_databases.why: The deploy log. Single source for both /restore and /updates, which is what stops those two pages drifting apart.

Inbound webmentions behind /inbox, plus the outbound send ledger. Deliberately NOT aadhar-restore: this is moderated, mutable content written by strangers, where checkpoints is the site's own append-only history.

vectorize_indexes.why: Passage index for the /lwe/ask RAG endpoint. Created once by hand; the create command survives only as a comment in that config.

workers.$comment: Worker inventory. `retired` is the interesting half: a Worker that should be gone but is not still holds its routes, and that is invisible from inside this repo.

expected.name: aadhar-sh
expected.why: The site Worker: homepage, Lens, coffee, Serendipity.

expected.name: cf-garage
expected.why: Intercepts /garage/cf/* ahead of the site Worker.

expected.name: lens-reader
expected.why: Intercepts /lens/read* ahead of the site Worker and serves the /lens Reader lens. SEPARATE because Readability needs a DOM Document, and linkedom supplying one costs 94.6 KB gzip on its own against a site bundle already over its 204.24 KiB budget. The second reason this note used to give, run_worker_first's 100-rule cap, EXPIRED when the eight exact /lens rows were folded to /lens + /lens/* and the config dropped to 94; the size reason is doing the work alone now. If this Worker goes missing, /lens keeps working and the Reader tab reports the extractor as unreachable.

retired.name: serendipity-collective
retired.why: The former Serendipity Worker. wrangler.jsonc now serves /serendipity* from the site Worker, so CLAUDE.md called for removing this one after the first successful production deploy. It was still deployed months later, which is what the first real run of the account tier caught. Deleted 2026-07-25 after confirming /serendipity still served 200 from the site Worker. The entry stays so the check keeps asserting it is gone: two deployments claiming overlapping surface, with the older one unversioned by this repo, is the state worth never returning to.

unmanaged.name: archie-kit-slack-oauth
unmanaged.why: Belongs to a different project on the same account. Listed so the check does not flag it as a stray.

$comment: The Cloudflare API tokens this repository depends on, and the scope each
one is allowed to hold. Declared for the same reason the rulesets are:
dashboard state that no config here can derive, load-bearing for what
reaches production, and silent when it changes. A token that quietly
regains account-wide Edit keeps every release working, so nothing goes
red on the day the blast radius grows.
WHY NOW. Cloudflare shipped granular Workers permissions on 2026-08-29:
four roles (Metadata Read-Only, Content Read-Only, Editor, Admin) that
can be granted at the platform, the product, or a SINGLE WORKER. Until
then `Workers Scripts:Edit` was the only write available and it covered
every Worker in the account, so the ramp token's breadth was a platform
limit rather than a choice. It is a choice now, which is what makes it
worth declaring.
THE ASYMMETRY, and it is the whole design. The RAMP token narrows to one
Worker cleanly. The CI READ token cannot go below the product, because
the Worker inventory section asks a question no scoped token can answer:
`workers.retired` asserts serendipity-collective is GONE and the stray
sweep asserts nothing undeclared appeared. Under a resource-scoped read,
a Worker missing from the listing and a Worker the token cannot see are
the same bytes, so both assertions would pass forever while measuring
nothing. That is precisely the shape check-infra.ts exists to refuse.
TIER: WORKSTATION, like repository.code_scanning and
zone.version_affinity. Reading a token's policies needs API Tokens Read,
which would let the CI credential enumerate every token on the account
and read its permissions. That is a WIDER grant than the one this block
exists to narrow, so CI degrades to a note and the assertion runs where
a broader credential already lives:
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=<a token carrying API Tokens Read> bun run infra:check
WHAT WAS MEASURED, 2026-08-29, and what was not. Both endpoints route on
this account and both accept Bearer auth: /accounts/<id>/tokens answers
9109 to a well-formed bogus token and /accounts/<id>/tokens/verify
answers 1000. Run UNAUTHENTICATED they answer 9106/9107 naming
X-Auth-Email and X-Auth-Key, which reads as `this endpoint wants the
Global API Key` and is wrong: that is just the no-auth default message.
The discriminator is a well-formed fake, and a malformed one is useless
because 6111 rejects the header before any auth path runs. Gotcha 41's
lesson through another door.
NOT measured: which scope the read actually costs, and the resource-key
string a resource-scoped Worker token carries. Neither is guessed here.
`resource_key` is null until the first run against a real token prints
what it observed; the checker reports the observed policy rather than
string-comparing against something nobody has seen.
So the hard failures are the two assertions that need no such string,
and both are stated as NEGATIVES on purpose:
read token   carries NO permission group that can write. Asserted
against the group NAME rather than against a declared
allowlist, on the bypass_actors precedent: a list invites
adding an entry to turn a red check green, which is the
exact change the check exists to catch. This is the prose
rule `if a token in this repo ever needs an Edit scope,
the answer is no` made machine-checkable.
ramp token   is NOT account-wide for Workers. Holding the bare account
resource means the narrowing was undone, whatever the new
permission groups end up being called.
permission_groups below are the DASHBOARD labels. The API's own names may
differ, so a mismatch there is reported and never fatal, and the report
prints the observed names so this block can be corrected from evidence.

expected.name: site-ci-read
expected.why: The six reads infra:check runs on. PRODUCT level rather than resource level, and that is a floor rather than a preference: the Worker inventory section reads the whole account listing to assert a retired Worker is gone and no stray appeared, and a resource-scoped token cannot tell absence from invisibility. Workers Scripts Read may become the granular Metadata Read-Only at product level, which is strictly narrower (the inventory reads ids and tags, never script code) and satisfies every assertion here.

expected.name: site-ramp
expected.location: GitHub environment secret on production-canary and production-full
expected.why: The only credential in this repository that can write, and it acts on exactly one Worker: deploy-promote.ts runs versions list, deployments status and versions deploy against aadhar-sh and nothing else. It carried account-level Workers Scripts Edit until granular permissions existed, which was edit rights over cf-garage, lwe-ask and lens-reader for a job that touches none of them. Editor rather than Admin because a ramp never creates or deletes a Worker, and Workers Routes is still not needed because it shifts traffic between versions that already exist.

expected.name: site-dns-write
expected.why: infra:apply's credential, declared here for completeness and unchecked by this section. It is zone-scoped rather than account-scoped, so it does not appear in an account token listing, and it deliberately never reaches CI: it can create and destroy zone-level DNS, which no pipeline here needs to do. Full reasoning lives in apply.token.

$comment_fields: checked            whether this section looks the token up at all. An
explicit flag rather than a read of `location`,
because the first draft filtered on location.includes
("GitHub") and the DNS token's location string is
"workstation only, never GitHub", which contains it.
The one token the filter was written to exclude was
the one it selected. Never let a prose field carry a
machine decision.
resource_scoped_group
the permission group that MUST be scoped below the
account, as a case-insensitive pattern. Only the
Workers half of the ramp token can be narrowed: D1
Edit and Account Settings Read have no per-resource
form, so they are account-wide of necessity and a
blunt `no policy may name the account` assertion can
never pass on a working token. It failed the clean
control on the first run, which is what a control is
for.
A pattern matching NO observed group is a hard
failure, not a pass. Cloudflare's API name for the
new roles is unmeasured here, so the guard can be
pointed at nothing by a rename, and a guard pointed
at nothing that reports success is the silent pass
this whole file exists to refuse. When it fires,
correct the pattern from the observed list the check
prints beside it.
tokens.write_group_pattern_note: Matched case-insensitively against each permission group's name. Cloudflare spells the write half of a permission `Write` in the API and `Edit` in the dashboard, and the granular Workers roles add `Admin`, so all three are caught. A group whose name matches this on a token declared may_write:false is a hard failure.

$comment: Policy for `bun run infra:apply`, the rebuild path. Everything else in
this file is read-only; this block is the one place that describes writes.
SCOPE: DNS records whose `match` is `exact`, and nothing else. That is not
an arbitrary line. `exact` is precisely the set where infra.json knows the
whole desired value, so it is the only set that can be recreated from this
file without inventing something. Everything excluded is excluded because
some other system is its rightful owner:
match: present   the DKIM key. Resend owns rotation and this file
deliberately does not pin the value, so it cannot
recreate it. Re-verify the domain in Resend instead.
match: proxied   the apex. Cloudflare creates and owns this record when
match: sameAs    the Worker custom domain is attached, so a rebuild gets
it from deploying the Worker, never from here.
resources        KV/R2/D1 creation mints NEW ids that would have to be
written back into wrangler.jsonc by hand. Wrangler
already creates these; see MAINTENANCE.md for the order.
the Worker       Workers Builds is the only publisher. Nothing here may
ever deploy it, or the release backstop is gone.
SAFETY: never runs in CI (a write token must not live in GitHub, which is
the whole reason production is unreachable from there). Prints a plan and
the exact API payloads before touching anything. Creates and updates only;
deleting needs --prune and is still confined to declared names, because an
undeclared record is more likely a third-party verification TXT than junk.
The plan itself needs NO credential: it diffs infra.json against public DNS
over DoH, same as the check. Only the write needs a token.
apply.ttl_note: 1 means Cloudflare 'automatic'. Public DNS reports remaining TTL rather than configured TTL, so the plan cannot diff TTL and does not try; it only sets TTL on records it creates.

token.why: A DELIBERATELY DIFFERENT env var from the read-only CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN the check uses. Two names means a write token can never be picked up by the check path by accident, and the read token in CI can never satisfy this one.

$comment: Zone settings that are load-bearing for something this repo does.
Checked as OBSERVED RESPONSES rather than as dashboard toggles, for two
reasons. A response needs no credential, so this runs on every PR with the
DNS tier. And a toggle can read `on` while a cache rule or page rule
overrides it for one path, so the response is the thing actually worth
asserting: what a visitor receives.
Only settings with a real consequence live here. Cloudflare exposes dozens
of zone toggles and almost all of them are defaults nobody has an opinion
about. Three of the five below are must-stay-OFF, which is the category
that rots quietest, because enabling a helpful-sounding feature never looks
like a regression at the time.
NOTE: this tier tests PRODUCTION, not the branch. A failure here is not
caused by the PR that surfaced it. The checker labels it accordingly.

checks.why: Cloudflare Polish would re-encode images at the edge, which would silently discard the entire encoder toolchain this repo maintains: zenc built from zenjpeg, 10-bit AVIF via avifenc, the q84 tuning, the 158-photo benchmark behind those choices. The site would look fine and every byte of that craft would be gone. Of everything checked here, this is the one that costs the most and shows the least.

Rocket Loader rewrites how scripts load, which would run straight over the deliberate discipline in index.html: the tiny inline tooltip loader, nav.js on defer, the speculation rules. The page is hand-tuned for its own load order.

The DNS-AID SVCB record advertises alpn=h2,h3. Turn HTTP/3 off at the zone and that record promises a protocol the edge does not speak, while the DNS check above stays green because the record itself never changed. Same cross-boundary shape as bimi.svg: two surfaces that only make sense together, and neither one alone can tell.

TLS 1.3 0-RTT session resumption: a returning visitor's request rides the resumption handshake itself, saving a full network round trip before the first response byte moves. With every payload on this site already at its compression floor, that round trip (tens of ms on a phone) is the largest per-visit latency lever left, and it is a dashboard toggle with no other representation in this tree — flipped off, nothing would notice while every repeat visit quietly got slower. Verified on 2026-07-30 by openssl probe: session tickets advertise max_early_data=14336 and a resumed connection's request sent as early data was accepted. Replay caveat, accepted deliberately: Cloudflare applies 0-RTT only to GET requests without query strings, and the one state-changing bare GET here is /hit, the noscript counter pixel — a replayed /hit inflates a vanity odometer and nothing else. The ?tick=1 beacon carries a query string and is excluded by construction, as are cal's signed approve/decline links.
checks.gotcha: The probe MUST hold the first connection open briefly after the request: TLS 1.3 delivers the session ticket AFTER the handshake, so a connect-and-hangup saves no ticket and the resumption test reads as a false rejection. Also, macOS system openssl is LibreSSL, whose s_client has no -early_data; the checker looks for a capable binary (homebrew openssl@3, or OPENSSL_BIN) and downgrades to a warning rather than reporting drift it cannot measure.
checks.pairs_with: http3-on above: h3 cuts the transport handshake for new connections, 0-RTT cuts it for resumed ones. Different visitors, same round trip.

checks.why: The performance budget is denominated in compressed bytes (CLAUDE.md pins the homepage at ~15.4KB zstd; perf-budget.mjs measures gzip and Brotli envelopes). Lose compression at the zone and those numbers quietly stop describing anything real, while perf-budget.mjs keeps passing because it compresses locally.

compression-on proves the edge CAN speak each encoding, one at a time. This proves which one it PICKS when a real browser offers all of them at once, which is the only version of the question a visitor ever experiences. Cloudflare's default preference is zstd, and its on-the-fly zstd is worse than its own on-the-fly brotli on this site's content: measured 2026-07-28 against /images/manifest.json, chosen because its 35,162-byte body is byte-identical every request while the homepage's is not (a random 12-photo grid moves the size ~1.4KB between renders, which is wider than the effect being measured). br 6,642 bytes, zstd 6,847: +205 bytes and +3.1%, paid by the majority of visitors, since Chrome and Edge both advertise zstd. The fix is a Compression Rule scoped to Default Content Types with the "Enable Brotli and Gzip Compression" preset, which drops zstd from the candidate list rather than merely ranking it lower; the recipe and the two form defaults to avoid live in MAINTENANCE.md. If Cloudflare's on-the-fly zstd ever overtakes its brotli, re-measure and flip the rule and this line together — the numbers here are something to re-run, not a constant to trust.

Cloudflare's default content-type list carries text/x-markdown, the pre-RFC name, and NOT text/markdown, the RFC 7763 type this site serves. So every Markdown surface shipped completely uncompressed until the Compression Rule went in: /index.md, /auth.md, /whoareyou.md, /bot.md and the src/content/md/ twins, 12,302 bytes that brotli takes to 5,943 — a 52% loss, measured 2026-07-28. It landed on exactly the surfaces built for agents and LLM crawlers, which fetch the .md representation by preference, and nothing in the tree noticed because no check had ever looked at a content type other than the homepage's. Serving text/x-markdown instead would win compression from the default list and is the wrong fix: it is deprecated, and agents expect the registered type. This check is the tripwire for the whole class, so if a new content type ever appears here, give it a target and a line.
checks.pairs_with: compression-prefers-brotli. That one asserts WHICH encoding is chosen; this one asserts that any is chosen at all. A rule scoped to Cloudflare's default content types would satisfy the first and fail this one.

checks.why: Exact-matched like SPF and DMARC above, because it is hand-chosen policy rather than a platform default. Weakening a preloaded policy is slow to undo, since browsers keep honouring the old max-age until it expires. Raising it is fine and should update this line. Raised from 15552000 (180d) to a full year on 2026-07-26: hstspreload.org rejects anything under 31536000 with max_age.below_1_year, so the `preload` token had been a claim the zone could not cash, and the domain was not on the list.

The repo declares these in _headers AND in the worker's SECURITY_HEADERS, and for an unknown stretch before 2026-07-26 the edge quietly overrode both: Cloudflare's `Add security headers` managed transform served x-frame-options SAMEORIGIN over the declared DENY, referrer-policy same-origin over strict-origin-when-cross-origin, plus two headers nobody asked for (expect-ct, an obsolete spec, and x-xss-protection: 1; mode=block, whose recommended value is now 0). Nothing in the repo could see it, because every local check reads the source rather than the wire. That is the whole argument for asserting observed responses: a header the code sets is not a header the visitor gets.

Cloudflare's WebMCP bridge is off in the dashboard (Agent Readiness, Labs) and src/client/webmcp.js registers this origin's tools instead, which is what carries the tool annotations the browser would otherwise drop and what gates a tool that writes behind a human. This check exists for the ORDER rather than for the toggle: /whoareyou and /security both state, in prose, that every script on the page is a file in this repository, and that claim is false for as long as the edge is still injecting. Dashboard first, prose second, exactly like the Workers Builds deploy command. Two things follow from the injection being edge-side. Re-enabling it in the dashboard silently makes two pages lie, and nothing in the tree could see that, which is the same argument app-owns-security-headers makes above. And the bridge never reached / at all, because that document is served as a dcz delta and HTMLRewriter cannot rewrite one, so the homepage registered zero tools while every other page registered 25 (gotcha 20 inverted).

index.html ships hand-tuned speculation rules with a deliberate exclusion list (/whoareyou keeps a per-request fingerprint honest, /rn* and /images* are endpoints and multi-megabyte R2 originals rather than pages). Speed Brain injected a second rule set over the top via this header: a blanket href_matches /* prefetch with no exclusions at all. Same failure shape as Polish above, where a helpful-sounding toggle silently overrides a deliberate choice the repo cannot see being overridden.

This site already answers `Accept: text/markdown` ITSELF, in the worker: wantsMarkdown() in _worker.js/lib/http.js does real q-value negotiation (markdown has to outrank html, which Cloudflare's zone feature does not check), and home.js plus serveMarkdownTwin serve committed or build-generated .md twins. Cloudflare's Markdown for Agents would convert HTML at the edge over the top of that, on every route, including the ones deliberately left without a twin. Same must-stay-off shape as Polish and Speed Brain above: a helpful-sounding toggle silently overriding a deliberate choice. The two assertions are the discriminator rather than decoration. x-markdown-tokens proves SOMETHING answered in markdown, so this fails loudly if the worker's own negotiation breaks instead of quietly passing on an HTML response. content-signal proves it was not Cloudflare: per the 2026-07-13 Markdown for Agents release the edge injects a default `content-signal: ai-train=yes, search=yes, ai-input=yes` whenever the origin sends none, and this origin sends none, because the policy lives in robots.txt. So that header appearing at all means the zone feature got switched on.

$comment: Workers Builds is the only production publisher for the site Worker, and its
settings are the release backstop.
THIS BLOCK IS NOW CHECKED, which it was not before 2026-08-04. The comment
here used to say there was no public REST endpoint for Workers Builds
configuration and that the checker CANNOT verify any of it, so the values
were recorded as intent alone and reviewed by hand. That is out of date:
Workers Builds has a REST API, the permission is `Workers Builds Configuration`, and it has a
READ variant — so verifying this costs a read-only scope and needs no
exception to the rule that nothing in this repo holds a token that can
write. check-infra.mjs reads the live triggers and fails on drift.
Add `Workers Builds Configuration:Read` to the CI token (a sixth read alongside Account
Settings, Workers Scripts, Workers KV Storage, Workers R2 Storage, and D1).
Without it the section degrades to a note naming the missing scope, same as
every other section, and the values fall back to being intent.
The dashboard's two command fields are two TRIGGERS in the API, told apart
by their branch filters: the one whose branch_includes holds "production"
is the dashboard's "Deploy command", and the other is its "Non-production
branch deploy command". Both are declared below.
The build_command MUST stay blank. wrangler.jsonc's build.command runs
build.mjs during `wrangler deploy`, so a non-empty field here builds twice,
and a field that runs something other than build.mjs is how production once
ended up serving an unminified 78KB nav.js.
BOTH deploy commands carry two hidden wrangler flags that DEFAULT TO
TRUE: --x-provision and --x-auto-create let a deploy create real KV/R2/D1
resources for any binding declared without an id. 4.114 relaxed the config
schema so more binding types can ship id-less, which makes that easier to
trip into. Resource IDs live in wrangler.jsonc and resources are created by
`bun run infra:apply` alone, so every deploy path is pinned off and a
missing id fails loudly instead of minting something nobody declared.
The NON-PRODUCTION command was the hole in that sentence until 2026-08-04.
It ran bare, so both flags took their default, and a push to ANY branch
could mint resources nobody declared. The rule was written down and still
missed it, because the rule ENUMERATED three deploy paths (`pnpm run
deploy:direct`, `bun run deploy:version`, and the dashboard Deploy command) while
a branch build is a fourth. Enumerating is what let one hide, so the
checks in check-infra.mjs now walk both commands from a single list.
A branch build is the worst place for this to sit rather than the most
harmless one. A feature branch is where an id-less binding gets written in
the first place, it publishes on every push with nobody watching, and the
Worker it publishes carries PRODUCTION bindings, since Cloudflare offers
no per-version override.
THE DEPLOY COMMAND UPLOADS A VERSION AND MOVES NO TRAFFIC. It is
`versions upload`, not `deploy`, which changes what a merge means: the
build runs, the assets upload, the secrets are checked, the Worker gets a
servable preview URL, and production keeps serving the version it was
already serving. Traffic moves when a human runs `bun run deploy:promote`
and ramps it. Merging is no longer the last step of a release.
The two provisioning flags survive the change, and that was VERIFIED
rather than assumed (2026-08-04): they are hidden, so --help does not
list them for either subcommand, and the way to tell whether `versions
upload` accepts them is that wrangler exits 1 on an unknown flag. It
exits 1 on --x-bogus-flag and 0 on --x-provision=false, so they are real
here. Re-run that control before trusting any flag --help omits.
`bun run deploy:direct` still exists and still deploys straight to 100%. It is
the fallback for the case CLAUDE.md documents at length: a fix for
production drift that infra:check can see cannot turn its own CI green
until it is live, and something has to break that cycle from outside.
$comment_npx: These two RECORD strings typed into the Cloudflare dashboard rather than
commands this repo runs, and check-infra.mjs compares them against the
live values. So editing either one here first fails the next infra:check
on drift it invented itself, and since `validate` is a required check,
that blocks its own merge. The order is dashboard FIRST, this file second.
Both moved from `npx` to `pnpm exec` on 2026-08-14, and then to the
wrapper above when the tree became bun, since one dashboard string has to
suit whichever shape the branch being built takes. Why leaving npx was
worth it, given `npx wrangler` was measured that same day resolving
pnpm's node_modules/.bin: npx FETCHES what it cannot resolve locally, so
a build whose install left no linked wrangler would publish production
with whatever version the registry hands it and say nothing. That is what
gotcha 29 measured in this repo's own scripts, npx answering 4.105.0
against a pinned 4.120.0, and `bun x` has the same hole. The wrapper runs
the pinned entry file under node and fetches nothing.
The one thing a workstation cannot verify is whether the Workers Builds
deploy shell can run these commands at all, and the proof is a branch build
publishing on it. If a future change to these commands touches something
the image supplies, stage it the same way: branch trigger first, since it
is the only trigger whose failure costs no release.

$comment: GitHub repository rulesets. This is the BRANCH half of the release model,
and it belongs here for the same reason the Workers Builds block does: it
is dashboard state no config in this repo can derive, it is load-bearing
for what may reach production, and its drift is silent.
It reads with NO CREDENTIAL, because the repo is public and the rulesets
endpoint is public with it. So this tier runs on every PR like the DNS
tier rather than degrading to a note like the account tier. Set
GITHUB_TOKEN for rate-limit headroom alone (60/hr unauthenticated per IP,
which shared Actions runners can exhaust); a rate-limited or unreachable
read is an ADVISORY, never a failure, so GitHub being down cannot redden a
PR that only touched CSS.
`visibility` is checked FIRST and is a precondition rather than a
preference. Rulesets on a private repo need a paid plan, so a repo flipped
back to private silently loses every rule below it. This file said the
opposite until 2026-08-05 (see CLAUDE.md, which carried the same stale
'free private-repo plan cannot enforce branch protection' premise), and a
flip back to private would restore that world without a word.
ZERO bypass actors is the load-bearing assertion on `main`. Claude, Codex
and every local worktree push with the OWNER's credentials, so a 'bypass
for repository admins' entry exempts precisely the actors the rule exists
to catch. bypass_actors is checked as EMPTY rather than as a declared list
on purpose: a list invites somebody to add an entry to this file to make a
red check go green, which is the failure the check exists to prevent.
`production` deliberately carries NO pull_request rule, and that absence is
asserted. promote-production.yml moves the ref with a PATCH carrying
force=false, and a PR rule there would break the release path outright.
Deletion + non_fast_forward buy one property: the release branch can only
move FORWARD, so Workers Builds cannot be handed a rewritten history. They
do NOT restrict WHO may push, so the workflow's own two guards (the commit
is still current main, and it belongs to a merged PR) remain the thing
keeping a non-CI commit off production. A ruleset governs refs; those
guards govern which commit may become a release.
ONE INTERACTION TO KNOW, and it resolves itself. CLAUDE.md documents
setting the `main` ruleset's enforcement to `disabled` for a single merge,
as the escape from the infra:check deadlock (a drift fix cannot turn green
until it is live, and `validate` is the required check gating it). While it
is disabled this section fails, so `validate` goes red, and that is
harmless, because a disabled ruleset is not requiring `validate` either. The
failure is then the tripwire for the real risk, which is nobody flipping it
back. Do NOT reach for a bypass actor instead: a standing exemption is
permanent and silent, while a disabled ruleset is loud here and shows up in
the audit log.
repository.name: site

rulesets.name: main
rulesets.why: 0 approvals because GitHub refuses to let anyone approve their own PR, so a solo repo requiring 1 could never merge. `validate` is pinned to integration_id 15368 (the GitHub Actions app) so only a real workflow run satisfies it and no caller of the commit-status API can. strict policy is FALSE so a Dependabot PR does not churn a rebase on every unrelated merge.

rulesets.name: production
rulesets.why: Forward-only, so Workers Builds cannot be handed a rewritten history. A pull_request rule here would break promote-production.yml, which is why its absence is asserted rather than merely unlisted.

$comment: CodeQL default setup. Same class as the rulesets above, and it arrived
here the same way: #241 curated this list, wrote the reasoning into
MAINTENANCE.md, and recorded that `infra:check` could not see it. That
sentence was true when written and is the exact shape of claim this file
exists to retire.
UNLIKE the rulesets, this one is WORKSTATION-ONLY, and structurally so.
The endpoint answers 401 unauthenticated even on a public repo, and the
permission it actually wants is the repository ADMINISTRATION read, which
is not among the keys a workflow may grant its GITHUB_TOKEN (actions,
artifact-metadata, attestations, checks, code-quality, contents,
deployments, discussions, id-token, issues, models, packages, pages,
pull-requests, repository-projects, security-events, statuses). So no
`permissions:` block can switch it on in CI.
`security-events: read` was added to ci.yml for exactly this and MEASURED
to do nothing: still HTTP 403 (2026-08-07). It has been removed, with a
note where it sat, because a permission that looks like it enables a check
and does not is worse than its absence. This is the mirror image of the
Workers Builds case above, where a Read variant of the permission existed
and made verification free. Here what reads it is any standing credential
carrying `repo`, which is the broad credential this repo deliberately keeps
out of CI, so the answer is no and the check runs where the owner runs it.
CI says so in one advisory rather than pretending.
A classic PAT is NOT the only such credential, and this comment said it
was. The gh CLI's own OAuth token qualifies, measured 2026-08-15: an
unauthenticated curl to this endpoint answers 401 and `gh api` answers
200 on a `gho_` token scoped `admin:public_key, gist, read:org, repo`.
The CI conclusion is untouched, since `repo` is the disqualifying scope
either way; what changes is that no PAT needs minting.
Being logged in buys nothing on its own, which is the trap.
check-infra.mjs reads process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN and never shells out to
gh, so a workstation with a good `gh auth login` still reports this tier
as an unverifiable 401. Hand it the token: `GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth
token) bun run infra:check`. Measured minutes apart on one machine, the
bare run printed the note and that line asserted the tier and caught a
real `state` drift.
WHAT DRIFT LOOKS LIKE HERE, and why each field is worth a check.
`languages` is the curated decision. #241 dropped `rust` and `python`
because between them they cost about 3 of the scan's 4 minutes to analyze
four files, all of it workstation and CI build tooling that never answers
a request. Re-enabling either from the Security tab silently buys that
cost back, and nothing in this tree would notice.
The list looks like four languages and is TWO jobs. `javascript`,
`javascript-typescript` and `typescript` are aliases GitHub keeps and
folds into one analysis. The declaration matches what the API returns
rather than the honest job count, because a checker comparing against the
prettier number would fail on a correct configuration.
`threat_model` is what makes the language argument valid. `remote` is why
build tooling that never answers a request is safely out of scope. Flip it
to include local and the case for dropping rust and python weakens, so a
silent change there would leave MAINTENANCE.md arguing from a premise the
dashboard no longer holds.
`state` is the one that matters most and is easiest to lose: `configured`
vs the scan simply being turned off. A disabled scanner reports nothing,
which reads identically to a clean scan.
`query_suite` is declared because `extended` is a large cost change that
somebody could reasonably click without meaning to make it permanent.
code_scanning.why: Advanced setup since 2026-08-15. TWO analysis jobs, and the omissions are the decision: rust and python were dropped 2026-08-06 (#241) as build tooling unreachable under the `remote` threat model. The old default-setup declaration listed four language names for the same two jobs, because that API reports `javascript`, `javascript-typescript` and `typescript` as aliases; a committed matrix has no aliases, so the list is now the honest job count.

$comment: The Actions policy: which actions may run, whether a third-party action
must be referenced by commit, and what the default GITHUB_TOKEN may do.
Same class as code_scanning above, and it arrived the same way: dashboard
state no config in this repo can derive, load-bearing for what runs in CI,
and silent when somebody changes it. Settings, then Actions, then General.
TWO OF THESE FOUR ARE DECLARED AHEAD OF REALITY, deliberately, so a
workstation run reports drift on them until the owner flips the toggle.
That is the precedent zone.version_affinity set: declare the state the
repo should be in and let the check name the gap, so a red line reads as a
to-do list rather than as a defect somebody introduced. Both flips are the
owner's separate act; nothing in this repository can perform them.
WORKSTATION-ONLY, for the same structural reason code_scanning is.
/repos/:slug/actions/permissions and .../permissions/workflow each answer
HTTP 401 unauthenticated on this public repo, measured 2026-08-27, so
neither joins the rulesets tier that runs on every pull request with no
credential. Run `GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) bun run infra:check` to
assert them; CI names the limit in one advisory and moves on.
`sha_pinning_required` is declared TRUE and is FALSE today. A tag is a
mutable pointer: `actions/checkout@v7` resolves to whatever the owner of
that repository last pushed there, so a tag reference is a standing grant
of arbitrary code execution inside CI to a third party who can change it
later without touching this tree. All 32 third-party references here are
already pinned to a 40-character commit by hand. The setting is what stops
the 33rd from arriving unpinned.
`default_workflow_permissions` is declared `read` and is `write` today,
and the flip costs NOTHING measurable, which is the argument for making
it. An explicit `permissions:` block always beats the repository default,
and all 14 workflows in .github/workflows carry one. The check COUNTS
that when it reports the drift rather than quoting this line, because
this sentence read "all 13" for a day while there were 14 and two of
the three copies of it were strings the script printed.
So today's `write` default governs exactly zero jobs. What it governs is
the NEXT workflow somebody adds without a block, which would silently
inherit write access to contents, issues, packages and pull requests.
`can_approve_pull_request_reviews` is declared TRUE and is TRUE today, and
it is the one entry here pointing the OTHER WAY: it guards against someone
turning a setting off rather than asking them to turn one on. Read the
field name with care, because it undersells what the checkbox does. The
dashboard control is `Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull
requests`, so clearing it stops the default GITHUB_TOKEN from CREATING a
pull request, and not only from approving one.
FOUR WORKFLOWS CREATE PULL REQUESTS with `gh pr create` on
`${{ github.token }}` and every one of them stops if this goes false:
dictionary-roll.yml:149, bun-pin.yml:183, og-cards.yml:149 and
photo-pipeline.yml:186. dictionary-roll is the expensive one. CLAUDE.md
records that the shell dictionaries went unrolled for 161 commits, that
`dcz:check` printed PASS throughout, and that a returning visitor was
taking 13.7 KB on the render-blocking path where the deltas are 1.3 KB.
The nightly roll is what closed that, and a cleared checkbox reopens it
with no error anywhere: `gh pr create` fails inside a scheduled job that
nobody is watching.
`allowed_actions` is declared `all` because it matches today and because
narrowing it is a real decision rather than a tidy-up. `selected` needs an
explicit allowlist of every action and every reusable workflow, which is a
second registry to maintain beside the pins above. Declared so that a
change to it is a diff rather than a surprise on the next CI run.
`pinned_action_refs` is the FREE half and is probably worth more than the
three API fields together, because it runs on every pull request with no
credential. It asserts from committed source that every action reference
under .github is already pinned to a 40-character commit, so an unpinned
action fails REVIEW rather than being rejected at run time by a setting
that is not switched on yet.
THE SCAN FAILS CLOSED, which is the property the number below does not
carry and cannot. A reference it cannot classify is an error naming the
file, the line and the text; three shapes evaded the first version and
each was reported as a clean pass. tools/lib/action-pins.ts holds the
scan and a contract test holds fixtures for all three.
$pinned_action_refs: The FLOOR on third-party action references under .github, and a floor
alone. 32 today, from 7 repositories across 8 paths, because
github/codeql-action contributes `init` and `analyze` from one commit.
WHAT THE FLOOR CATCHES is a scan that stopped matching, which is a real
failure this repository has shipped more than once: a pattern that
matches nothing reports a clean pass, and a control confirmed this one
reads 0 of 24 when the matcher breaks. The 8 of slack absorbs deleting a
workflow or two without churn.
WHAT IT CANNOT CATCH is an evasion, and believing otherwise is what let
three of them through. A hidden unpinned reference moves this count by
zero or by one, so no threshold separates a clean repository from a
compromised one. Coverage is held by the scan failing CLOSED on anything
it cannot classify, and by the fixtures in
tools/contract-every-action-reference-under-github-is-pinned.test.mjs.
Local `./` references are RESOLVED, never exempted. There are 12 and each
one has its target action file located and scanned, transitively, which
is what covers a composite nested below .github/actions or living outside
the directory entirely. A target that cannot be found fails. The old note
here said a path reference has no upstream owner and so needs no check;
that is true of the reference and false of the file it points at.
actions_permissions.why: Declared 2026-08-27. Three API fields on two workstation-only endpoints, plus a tree-tier assertion that needs no credential. sha_pinning_required and default_workflow_permissions are declared ahead of live state on purpose and report drift until the owner flips them in Settings, then Actions, then General.

$comment: Secret scanning and its companions, read off the repository's own
`security_and_analysis` object. Declared here rather than trusted for the
reason every block in this file is: five independent toggles in a
dashboard, each of which fails by reporting nothing.
NAMED AFTER THE API OBJECT rather than after secret scanning, which is
what it was called for a day. The check reads every key on that object,
and `dependabot_security_updates` is one of them: filing a Dependabot
setting under a block called `secret_scanning` is the kind of small lie
that makes the next reader distrust the whole file.
NO EXTRA API CALL. checkRepo already fetches /repos/:slug for the
`visibility` precondition, and `security_and_analysis` rides on that same
payload when the request is authenticated. It is ABSENT from the anonymous
response entirely, measured 2026-08-27: that endpoint answers HTTP 200
without a credential and simply omits the key, which is a sharper trap
than the 401s above, because a checker written against the anonymous shape
sees a successful read of an object with nothing in it. So this tier is
workstation-only like code_scanning, and a missing key is reported as
unverifiable rather than as four settings being off.
`secret_scanning` and `secret_scanning_push_protection` are both enabled
today and are declared to hold that. Push protection is the half that acts
rather than reports: it refuses the push that carries a credential, which
is worth far more than an alert filed after the secret is in the history
of a PUBLIC repository, where the correct response is rotation rather than
a rewrite.
`secret_scanning_non_provider_patterns` is declared DISABLED, and was
declared enabled from 2026-08-27 until 2026-08-30 as a deliberate
tripwire waiting for the owner to flip it. IT CANNOT BE FLIPPED ON THIS
ACCOUNT. GitHub gates the feature on organization-owned repositories on
Team or Enterprise Cloud with GitHub Secret Protection; this repo is
user-owned, and its Settings, Advanced Security page renders no row for
it, offering Secret Protection and Push protection alone.
What it would buy, kept here for the day this moves to an org: the
default scan matches partner patterns, meaning tokens whose shape a
provider has registered with GitHub. What it misses is the generic
material: private keys, connection strings, and anything hand-rolled.
This repository holds an Ed25519 signing key for AadharshBot whose public
half ships at /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory, and it
carries SIGNING_SECRET, RESEND_API_KEY, ICAL_URL and BROWSER_RUN_TOKEN as
Worker secrets. None of those is a partner pattern. The cost is false
positives, which land as alerts the owner dismisses.
`dependabot_security_updates` is declared enabled and is enabled today.
It is here because it was LIVE AND UNDECLARED when this block was first
written, and nothing said so: the check looped over the keys this file
names, which answers "is every setting I declared still right" and
cannot answer "what else is on this object". A live key with no
declaration is now an advisory, matching the undeclared-ruleset line in
checkRepo.
`secret_scanning_validity_checks` is declared DISABLED for the same
reason and with one extra: it is not a field on the update-repository
endpoint at all. That reference lists nine `security_and_analysis` keys
and this is not among them, so no request can set it even where the
feature is sold. The Advanced Security page renders no row for it either.
What it would buy: it asks the provider whether a leaked token still
works, which turns an alert into a decision, since an active credential is
an incident and an expired one is cleanup. Worth reading before flipping
it if it ever becomes available, because it sends the detected token to
the issuing provider to be validated. Every partner credential this
repository could leak belongs to Cloudflare, GitHub or Resend, all of
which already hold the token in question.
MEASURED 2026-08-30, and the measurement is the part to keep. PATCH
/repos/oddharsh/site setting either field answers HTTP 200 with the full
repo object and changes nothing, on a token carrying `repo` against a repo
reporting `permissions.admin: true`. So the 200 is not evidence the write
landed. The control that settles it: the same endpoint accepts
`security_and_analysis.definitely_not_a_real_field_xyz` with an identical
200, so it silently swallows anything it does not act on. Read this the
way the wrangler `--x-bogus-flag` control is read elsewhere in this repo,
and do not retry the PATCH: it will keep answering 200.
security_and_analysis.why: Declared 2026-08-27, corrected 2026-08-30. Read off the repo metadata checkRepo already fetches, so it costs no extra call. All five now match live state: non-provider patterns and validity checks were declared ahead of it as a tripwire for the owner, and both turn out to be unreachable on a user-owned repo without GitHub Secret Protection, so the tripwire was a check nobody could clear. A live key this block does not name is an advisory, so GitHub adding a sixth is a declaration to write rather than a red pull request. Should either become available, enabling it is a declaration to change here in the same commit.

$comment: The GitHub triage surface: who a new issue or pull request is assigned
to, and which labels describe it. Declared here for the same reason the
rulesets above are: it is dashboard state no config in this repo can
derive, and its drift is silent.
SILENT IS LITERAL, and it is the whole reason this is checked rather
than trusted. POST /issues/:n/labels CREATES a label that does not
exist, picking a colour for it, so a typo in a routing rule does not
error: it mints `area: garagee` in the repository's label set and the
pull request looks correctly triaged. Nothing anywhere reports it.
THE ROUTING RIDES ALONG WITH THE DECLARATION, on purpose, though only
the colour and description halves are remote state. Splitting them puts
the label names in two files, and then the two failures this block
exists to catch are both reintroduced from the other side: a label
nothing can ever apply, and a route naming a label that was never
declared. One file lets check-infra assert BOTH directions with no
network call, and the live diff is what it adds on top.
`title` matches the conventional-commit prefix a pull request title
already carries (`fix(photos):` gives `type: fix`). `paths` matches the
changed files. One axis each, deliberately: the title says what kind of
change it is and the diff says where it lands, so each source is asked
the question it can actually answer.
TWO LABELS ARE NOT TAXONOMY AND ARE THE REASON TO DO THIS AT ALL.
`hashed-asset` fires on the client and style sources build.ts content-
hashes into /a/, which is gotcha 35: touching one remints every page
that references it, every page dictionary, _headers and shell-assets,
so the diff arrives at ~1400 files and usually owes a dictionary roll.
`release-path` fires on the files that decide what reaches production.
Both are facts a reviewer wants BEFORE opening the diff, and neither is
legible from a title.
`assignee` is asserted against the workflow rather than against GitHub,
because assignment is per-issue state with nothing repository-wide to
read back. What the check buys there is that the workflow and this file
cannot disagree about who owns the inbox.
ONE PLATFORM LIMIT, and it is why some workflows carry `--label` inline.
An event created with the default GITHUB_TOKEN does not trigger another
workflow, so the three self-opened pull requests here (dictionary-roll,
bun-pin, og-cards) and the node-support-window issue never reach
triage.yml. They label and assign themselves at creation instead, which
is also why a label they name MUST exist: `gh pr create --label` fails
outright on an unknown one, so a rename here without a sync breaks the
nightly roll rather than mislabelling it. check-infra reads those flags
out of the workflows and fails on any label they name that this file
does not declare.
Strays WARN rather than fail, matching the ruleset tier: GitHub ships a
stock label set on every repository, and failing on labels nobody chose
would make the first run of this check red for something that is not a
defect. `bun run labels:sync -- --confirm --prune` removes them when you
mean to, and a deletion strips the label from every issue and pull
request that carried it, historically and with no undo.
$self_labelling_workflows: The FLOOR on inline `--label` flags across .github/workflows, not a
count. Four workflows label themselves at creation because triage.yml
cannot see them (dictionary-roll, bun-pin, og-cards, node-support-
window), and they carry two flags each, so eight is the real number.
Six is the floor because a scanner that matches nothing reports a
clean pass, which is how every naive scanner in this repo has failed.
Losing a whole workflow's pair trips it; adding or removing one label
$dependabot_ecosystems: The FLOOR on `package-ecosystem:` list items in .github/dependabot.yml,
and it is STRUCTURAL rather than an inventory. check-infra reads that
file's `labels:` lists and fails on a name this block does not declare,
because Dependabot REPLACES its default labels with that list and drops
an unknown name in silence: #620 shipped carrying no `dependencies`
label at all, against a `github-actions` label GitHub never had.
A line scanner that stops matching this file's shape finds zero labels
and reports a clean pass, so the floor asserts the file parsed. Five
ecosystems today (npm, github-actions, pip, cargo, npm again for
lens-reader); four is the floor, so deleting one block is a deliberate
act that costs nothing here while a broken parser matches zero and fails.

labels.name: hashed-asset
labels.description: Remints an /a/ URL, so every page and page dictionary rebuilds
labels.why: gotcha 35. A cosmetic edit to a content-hashed client asset moves its /a/<name>.<hash8> URL, which remints every page that references it, every per-page dictionary, _headers and shell-assets.ts. The diff arrives at ~1400 files and usually owes a dictionary roll. A comment-only edit is free, because oxc-minify strips it and the hash holds. The globs are deliberately a SUPERSET of build.ts's ASSETS list: every hashed asset authors in one of these three places, and matching the directory rather than the eight filenames means a ninth entry inherits the warning instead of quietly missing it. The cost of the superset is a label on an edit to an unhashed island, which over-warns; the cost of an exact list is silence on the one case the label exists for.
